children.name: Glossopetalon pungens Brandegee
children.description: Glossopetalon pungens Brandegee — a dense, intricately branched deciduous shrub, 15–25 cm tall, with spine-tipped leaves and solitary terminal white flowers (petals 6–8 mm, stamens 10). Narrowly endemic to limestone substrates in San Bernardino County, California and adjacent Clark, Lincoln, and Nye counties, Nevada, at 1675–2000 m elevation in chaparral and pinyon-juniper woodland. Resolved as sister to all other Glossopetalon species in molecular phylogenies. NatureServe G2 (Imperiled) due to restricted range and specialized habitat.

children.name: Velascoa recondita Calderón & Rzed.
children.description: Velascoa recondita Calderón & Rzed. — a rupicolous (rock-dwelling) prostrate or hanging shrub up to 1 m long, with microphyllous, coriaceous leaves and a distinctive elongate, narrowly funnelform hypanthium unique within Crossosomataceae. Narrowly endemic to a single locality near Lagunita de San Diego, Landa de Matamoros, Querétaro, Mexico, where it grows in cracks and small caves within limestone boulders on steep, vertical cliffs in humid pine-white cedar-oak forest at 2250–2650 m. Extent of occurrence less than 10 km². Flowers in August, fruits in November. Described as a new genus and species in 1997 by Calderón & Rzedowski; the specific epithet recondita means 'hidden'.

children.name: Crossosoma bigelovii S.Watson
children.description: Crossosoma bigelovii, known by the common name ragged rockflower, is one of only a few species in the flowering plant family Crossosomataceae.

children.name: Crossosoma bigelowii S.Watson
children.description: Crossosoma bigelowii S.Watson — a spelling variant of C. bigelovii, the ragged rockflower, a deciduous, much-branched spinescent shrub 1–2 m tall with rigid, thorny branchlets and small gray-green leaves. Produces fragrant, apple blossom-like white to pinkish flowers in late winter to early spring (February–April). Native to the Mojave, Sonoran, and Chihuahuan Deserts of southeastern California, southern Nevada, western Arizona, and northwestern Mexico (Baja California, Sonora, Chihuahua), growing on dry rocky slopes and cliff crevices at 150–1400 m. Flowers have a glandular disk lining the hypanthium and numerous stamens; fruit is a horizontally wrinkled follicle with black seeds bearing a fringed white aril.
